Input validation and sanitization for untrusted data WHAT: Failing to validate and sanitize untrusted input at every application tier and only accepting data by default can lead to injection and other attacks. WHY: Unchecked user-controlled data is a primary cause of injection vulnerabilities (e.g., OWASP Top 10), data corruption, and integrity issues across systems. HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted by default; classify data sources as trusted/untrusted; apply allowlist-based validation (whitelisting, boundary checks, numeric checks, table lookups, uniqueness and referential integrity checks) on the server; then sanitize (e.g., invalid UTF-8, HTML tags, `<` characters, control/extra whitespace, unsafe octets) before use or storage. EXAMPLE: Before: accept and process request parameters directly in business logic and database queries. After: on the server, first validate each parameter against strict type/length/format and allowed values, enforce consistency checks, then sanitize text fields to remove/encode dangerous characters before using them. Input Validation for User-Supplied Data WHAT: Failing to validate and reject unexpected or malformed user input allows invalid or malicious data to enter the system. WHY: Unvalidated input can lead to security vulnerabilities, data corruption, and integrity issues across interconnected systems and applications. HOW: For all user-controlled data, perform strict validation against expected formats and types (e.g., using Go’s strconv, strings, regexp, and utf8 packages) and reject any input that does not meet these criteria. EXAMPLE: Before: accept raw string input and use it directly in logic or storage. After: use strconv.Atoi for numeric fields, regexp to enforce allowed patterns, and utf8.ValidString to ensure valid UTF-8, returning an error on validation failure. Input Validation and Data Integrity WHAT: Failure to robustly validate and normalize user-controlled input (including form fields, file paths, headers, and cross-system data) can allow injection, path traversal, malformed encoding abuse, and data corruption. WHY: Insufficient validation enables attackers to bypass security checks, access or overwrite unintended files, manipulate requests/responses, and tamper with data integrity across systems and databases. HOW: Enforce strict allowlist validation for all external input; check lengths and numeric ranges; escape special characters; reject null bytes, newline characters, path-alteration sequences (../, \\..), and non-ASCII in HTTP headers; detect/normalize extended UTF-8; validate file paths and existence before access; and apply integrity checks (hash totals, cross-system consistency, referential integrity, uniqueness). EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `filename := r.FormValue("file"); data, _ := os.ReadFile("/data/" + filename)` After (safer): `filename := r.FormValue("file"); if !validName(filename) || strings.Contains(filename, "..") { return error }; full := filepath.Join("/data", filename); if !fileExists(full) { return error }; data, _ := os.ReadFile(full)` Post-validation data handling WHAT: Failing to define and apply appropriate post-validation actions can lead to insecure handling of user input, including silent modification or acceptance of problematic data. WHY: Improper post-validation handling may cause data loss (e.g., truncation), inconsistent state, or security issues when invalid or altered data is stored or used. HOW: After validation, explicitly choose and implement one of: (1) Enforcement: reject invalid data and clearly inform the user; (2) Safe server-side modification only for non-sensitive, cosmetic fields; (3) Advisory/Verification: accept data but warn or ask the user to confirm or adjust it, especially for critical fields. EXAMPLE: N/A HTML sanitization and tag stripping in Go WHAT: Improper or incomplete sanitization of user-controlled HTML (e.g., using html.EscapeString but not encoding all relevant characters, or failing to strip dangerous tags) can leave injection vectors such as XSS in templates or responses. WHY: Attackers can inject scripts or malicious markup into web pages, leading to XSS, data theft, session hijacking, or content spoofing. HOW: After validating input, escape HTML using html.EscapeString for basic characters and, when broader coverage is needed, use a well-maintained third-party sanitizer that encodes all relevant characters and/or safely strips tags (e.g., bluemonday). Do not rely on unexported or partial stripping logic; consistently sanitize or strip all user-controlled HTML before rendering. EXAMPLE: In Go, instead of manually replacing only "<" and ">", use a sanitizer library such as bluemonday to process user input before inserting it into html/template output. ServeMux CONNECT path sanitization WHAT: When using net/http.ServeMux, the URL path of CONNECT requests is not sanitized or cleaned, which can allow unsafe “.”, “..”, or similar segments to be processed and enable path traversal. WHY: Unsanitized CONNECT paths can let attackers access files or endpoints outside the intended directory or routing scope, leading to data exposure or unauthorized actions. HOW: Either disallow or strictly limit CONNECT methods at the server or handler level, or explicitly normalize and validate any CONNECT request paths (e.g., reject paths containing “..” or non-canonical segments) before use. EXAMPLE: Before: allowing all methods on a handler that uses r.URL.Path directly for file or route resolution. After: explicitly reject CONNECT in middleware or handler, or sanitize and validate r.URL.Path for CONNECT before using it. Output Encoding Policy for Injection Prevention WHAT: Failing to properly encode untrusted data before outputting it in a specific context (e.g., HTML, JavaScript, SQL) allows injection vulnerabilities when that data is interpreted as code or markup. WHY: Attackers can inject and execute arbitrary code, steal data, deface content, or compromise user accounts and backend systems. HOW: For every output sink, apply context-appropriate encoding to all untrusted data (from users, databases, third-party services) using well-vetted libraries; never concatenate raw untrusted data into code/markup; define and enforce a consistent output-encoding policy across the application. EXAMPLE: (web, HTML context) Before: `
${userInput}
` After (Java): `
${StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml4(userInput)}
` Cross-Site Scripting in HTTP Responses WHAT: Failing to escape or validate user-supplied input before including it in HTTP responses (e.g., writing r.URL.Query().Get("param1") directly to the response) can lead to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). WHY: Attackers can inject and execute arbitrary scripts in victims’ browsers, enabling session theft, credential harvesting, defacement, or arbitrary actions on behalf of users. HOW: Treat all user-controlled data as untrusted; validate it server-side (prefer allowlists) and always HTML-escape it before including it in pages. In Go, use html/template for HTML output instead of writing raw strings, and set an appropriate Content-Type explicitly. EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable, Go): io.WriteString(w, r.URL.Query().Get("param1")) After (safer, Go): tmpl := template.Must(template.New("p").Parse("{{.}}")); tmpl.Execute(w, r.URL.Query().Get("param1")) Validate HTML-like prefixes in user-controlled parameters WHAT: If param1 begins with "

", the response Content-Type is set to text/html, potentially treating untrusted data as HTML. WHY: Misclassifying untrusted content as HTML can enable cross-site scripting (XSS) and content injection attacks. HOW: Do not derive Content-Type solely from user-controlled prefixes; instead, determine Content-Type based on server-side logic and validate/encode any user input included in HTML responses. EXAMPLE: Before: if (param1.startsWith("

")) res.setHeader("Content-Type","text/html"); After: res.setHeader("Content-Type","text/plain"); res.send(escapeHtml(param1)); XSS when rendering unsanitized HTML in HTTP responses WHAT: Rendering user-controlled values directly into HTML responses (e.g., via templates or automatic Content-Type detection) allows execution of injected scripts such as ``. WHY: Attackers can perform Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), leading to session theft, account takeover, data exfiltration, or arbitrary actions in the victim’s browser. HOW: Treat all user input as untrusted; use an HTML-aware escaping/sanitization library (e.g., html/template or equivalent) for every untrusted value rendered into HTML, and never rely on Content-Type defaults or text/plain/text-template alone for safety. EXAMPLE (Go): Before: `fmt.Fprintf(w, param1)` with `w.Header().Set("Content-Type","text/html")`; After: `tmpl := template.Must(template.New("p").Parse("{{.}}")); tmpl.Execute(w, param1)` which auto-escapes HTML. Use html/template instead of text/template for untrusted HTML output WHAT: Using text/template to render untrusted user input into HTTP responses can result in raw HTML being sent (e.g., when input contains tags like "

"), enabling cross-site scripting (XSS). WHY: Attackers can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into the page, leading to session theft, data exfiltration, or arbitrary actions in the user’s browser. HOW: For any HTTP response that may contain user-controlled content, use html/template (which auto-escapes HTML) instead of text/template; never write unescaped user input directly to the response body. EXAMPLE (Go, before): import "text/template" ... tmpl := template.New("hello") ... tmpl.ExecuteTemplate(w, "T", param1) EXAMPLE (Go, after): import "html/template" ... tmpl := template.New("hello") ... tmpl.ExecuteTemplate(w, "T", param1) Unclear or misleading XSS-safety assumptions WHAT: Assuming user-controlled HTML-like input is always safe because a template engine auto-escapes it, without explicitly verifying the escaping/encoding behavior for the target context. WHY: Misunderstanding escaping guarantees can lead to stored or reflected XSS if the data is later rendered in a different context (e.g., HTML attributes, JS, or with escaping disabled). HOW: Explicitly document and verify the template engine’s escaping rules; never disable auto-escaping for user input; re-validate and re-encode data when moving it to a new context (HTML, JS, JSON, attributes, URLs). EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe assumption): “param1 is safe everywhere because template escapes it.” After: Treat `param1` as untrusted, and for each use, ensure context-appropriate encoding (e.g., HTML-escape for HTML body, JS-string-escape for inline JS). SQL Injection Prevention WHAT: Building SQL queries by concatenating user-controlled input directly into the query string allows arbitrary SQL to be injected and executed by the database. WHY: Attackers can bypass authorization, read or modify sensitive data (e.g., all credit cards), or destroy data, leading to full database compromise. HOW: Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL; instead, use parameterized queries/prepared statements with placeholders and bind all external values as parameters, following the placeholder syntax of your specific database/driver. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): query := "SELECT number FROM creditcards WHERE customerId = " + customerId After (safe): query := "SELECT number FROM creditcards WHERE customerId = ?"; db.QueryContext(ctx, query, customerId) Centralized Authentication and Credential Management WHAT: Failing to centralize authentication, using untrusted or ad‑hoc mechanisms, or storing external service credentials in source code or unprotected locations on untrusted systems. WHY: Leads to bypassable authentication, increased attack surface, credential theft, and unauthorized access to sensitive data or functions. HOW: Enforce all authentication on a trusted backend; use standard, well-tested framework authentication modules; review them for malicious or insecure code; centralize authentication with safe local-only redirects; store external service credentials encrypted in protected server-side locations, never in source code. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): application code embeds API keys in source and performs its own login checks per resource. After (secure): framework’s authentication module runs on the backend as a single control point; resources redirect to it, and API keys are loaded from an encrypted server-side secrets store. Secure handling of authentication data in web applications WHAT: Authentication data is exposed if passwords are visible on screen, stored via “remember me”/autocomplete, sent over unencrypted HTTP, included in URLs/query strings, or if error messages reveal whether username or password is incorrect. WHY: Leaked credentials and detailed error feedback enable credential theft, brute-force optimization, and user impersonation. HOW: Use ``, disable “remember me”/browser autocomplete for credentials, send credentials only via HTTPS using HTTP POST (never in URLs/query strings), and return a single generic error message for all authentication failures. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `
` After (secure): `
` Authentication error handling and timing-attack-safe password comparison WHAT: Revealing whether a username exists via distinct error messages and using naive string comparison for passwords can leak valid accounts and enable timing attacks. WHY: Attackers can enumerate registered users and infer correct passwords by measuring response-time differences, leading to account takeover. HOW: Always return a generic authentication error (e.g., “Invalid credentials”) regardless of whether the username exists or the password is wrong; use constant-time comparison functions for password checks and invoke them even when the user record is missing (e.g., compare against an empty value). EXAMPLE: Before: if (!user) return "User not found"; if (user.pw == inputPw) login(); After: fetchedHash = user ? user.pwHash : emptyHash; if (ConstantTimeCompare(fetchedHash, Hash(inputPw))) login(); else return "Invalid credentials". Secure password storage with salts WHAT: Storing raw or simply hashed passwords without per-user salts allows attackers to use rainbow tables and identify shared passwords across accounts after a database leak. WHY: If an attacker obtains the authentication database, unsalted or weakly hashed passwords can be efficiently cracked and reused for account takeover and credential stuffing. HOW: Never store plaintext passwords; instead, store only the result of a strong one-way password hashing function (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) applied to a unique, high-entropy salt plus the password for each user. EXAMPLE: Before: `stored_password = sha256(user_password)`; After: `salt = generate_random_salt(); stored_password = bcrypt_hash(salt + user_password)` and store both `salt` and `stored_password`. Password hashing and salting WHAT: Storing passwords as a simple hash of salt+password using a fast general-purpose hash (e.g., SHA-256, SHA-1, MD5) is insecure; attackers can brute-force or use precomputed tables efficiently. WHY: Compromise of the password store allows rapid offline cracking of user passwords, leading to account takeover and broader system compromise. HOW: Use a dedicated, slow, memory-hard password hashing function (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) with a unique, randomly generated salt per password; store the salt in plaintext alongside the hash; configure work factor/iterations to be expensive but acceptable for your environment. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `hash = sha256(salt || password)`; After (secure, Go): `hash, err := argon2.IDKey(password, salt, time, memory, threads, keyLen)` and store `(hash, salt, params)` in the database. Secure password storage with vetted hashing algorithms WHAT: Storing plaintext or weakly-hashed passwords (e.g., custom crypto, fast hashes) instead of using a strong, salted password hashing function like bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2, or scrypt. WHY: Weak or custom password storage allows attackers who obtain the database to quickly recover user passwords, leading to account takeover and credential stuffing across other services. HOW: Never design your own password hashing; use well-reviewed libraries (e.g., golang.org/x/crypto) and algorithms (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2, scrypt) with appropriate cost parameters, and store only the resulting hash (and salt/parameters), not the plaintext password. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure, Go): `db.Exec("INSERT INTO accounts(password) VALUES(?)", password)`; After (secure, Go): `hash, _ := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword(password, bcrypt.DefaultCost); db.Exec("INSERT INTO accounts(hash) VALUES(?)", hash)`. Use maintained password-hashing libraries with safe defaults WHAT: Using custom or outdated password hashing/comparison logic can lead to weak, misconfigured, or incorrect password verification. WHY: Improper password handling increases the risk of credential theft, offline cracking, and account compromise. HOW: Delegate password hashing and comparison to a well-reviewed, actively maintained library with safe defaults (e.g., bcrypt/argon2 wrappers), and regularly check for known vulnerabilities in that package. EXAMPLE: Before: Manually hashing and comparing passwords with ad‑hoc crypto and parameters. After: Use a dedicated password library that exposes functions like `HashPassword()` and `ComparePassword()` with secure, preconfigured algorithms and parameters. Password and Reset Policy WHAT: Weak, reused, or poorly managed passwords and insecure reset flows (e.g., trivial security questions, long‑lived reset links, unverified email targets) allow attackers to take over accounts. WHY: Compromised passwords can lead to unauthorized access across multiple services, data breaches, and persistent account hijacking. HOW: Enforce password complexity and minimum length (e.g., ≥16 chars or multi-word passphrases), require periodic changes and prevent reuse (including minimum password age ≥1 day), and implement secure reset flows: send temporary links/passwords only to pre-registered emails, with short expiry, notify users on reset, force change on first use, and use reset questions that allow high-entropy, non-obvious answers. EXAMPLE: Before: Accept any password and allow unlimited immediate changes; send permanent reset links to any provided email. After: Require strong passwords and track history/age; send short-lived reset tokens only to the stored email, notify the user, and force a new strong password on next login. Authentication hardening guidelines WHAT: Weak or missing authentication controls (no re-auth, MFA, lockouts, monitoring, or default-credential changes) allow attackers to hijack or brute-force accounts. WHY: Leads to account takeover, unauthorized critical actions, and large-scale credential attacks, including bypass of simple lockout mechanisms. HOW: Re-authenticate users before critical operations; require MFA for high-value accounts; monitor for password reuse across many accounts; change or disable all vendor default credentials; enforce temporary account lockouts after a small number of failed logins. EXAMPLE: Before: `if (checkPassword(user, pass)) performWireTransfer();` After: `if (checkPassword(user, pass) && reauthenticate(user, currentPassword)) performWireTransfer();` Secure session token and cookie management WHAT: Session identifiers may be predictable or cookies may be misconfigured (missing HttpOnly/Secure, improper domain/path/expiry), enabling session hijacking or brute forcing. WHY: Attackers can guess or steal tokens to impersonate users, escalate privileges, or maintain unauthorized access. HOW: Generate session tokens using cryptographically secure randomness and strong signing keys; never hard-code secrets; set cookies with appropriate Domain, Path, short Expires/Max-Age, and always enable HttpOnly and Secure; issue and validate sessions only on trusted server-side components. EXAMPLE (Go): Before: `signedToken, _ := token.SignedString([]byte("secret")); cookie := http.Cookie{Name:"Auth",Value:signedToken}`; After: `key := loadKeyFromSecureStore(); signedToken, err := token.SignedString(key); cookie := http.Cookie{Name:"Auth",Value:signedToken,Path:"/",Domain:"example.com",HttpOnly:true,Secure:true,Expires:time.Now().Add(30*time.Minute)}`. Secure Session and Cookie Management WHAT: Improper session handling (reusing sessions, exposing IDs in URLs, weak tokens, missing logout) can allow session hijacking and unauthorized access. WHY: Attackers can steal or brute-force session identifiers, perform MITM attacks, or reuse active sessions to impersonate users and access sensitive data. HOW: Always create a new session on sign-in; enforce session expiration; prevent concurrent logins per username; store session IDs only in secure HTTP cookies (not in URLs/GET params); protect session data from other server users; use HTTPS for all authenticated requests; generate cryptographically strong, sufficiently long tokens (per-request for highly sensitive actions); and fully invalidate server- and client-side session data on logout. EXAMPLE (Go): Before: `http.ListenAndServe(":80", nil)` and `?sid=123` in URL. After: `err := http.ListenAndServeTLS(":443", "cert/cert.pem", "cert/key.pem", nil)` and use `cookie, err := req.Cookie("Auth")` with no session identifiers in query parameters. Access control implementation WHAT: Improper or inconsistent access control (e.g., trusting unvalidated tokens, missing checks on some endpoints) allows unauthorized users to access protected resources, URLs, functions, or data. WHY: Attackers can escalate privileges, access sensitive data, or invoke protected operations, compromising confidentiality and integrity. HOW: Use a single, centralized authorization component; base decisions only on trusted server-side objects (e.g., validated JWTs); enforce authorization on every request (including AJAX/Flash/server-side scripts); fail closed on any configuration or authorization failure; and keep privileged logic clearly separated from non-privileged code. EXAMPLE: Before: Each handler checks user role differently or not at all, sometimes trusting raw request parameters. After: All handlers call a shared `Authorize(request, requiredPermission)` function that validates the JWT, loads policy from configuration, and denies access by default on any error. Access Control and Session Authorization Consistency WHAT: Inconsistent or weak access control and session authorization, including mismatched server/UI rules, client-side state tampering, over-privileged accounts, and failure to re-check or revoke authorization during long sessions. WHY: Leads to unauthorized access, privilege escalation, data tampering, and potential Denial-of-Service (DoS) via excessive transactions. HOW: Enforce access control only on the server; ensure UI reflects server rules; encrypt and integrity-protect any client-stored state; implement rate limits per user/device; never rely solely on the Referer header; periodically re-check user authorization during long sessions and force re-authentication on change; support account auditing, disabling, and session termination on revocation; use least privilege for all external/service accounts. EXAMPLE: Before: `if (request.headers['referer'] === trustedUrl) allowTransfer();` After: `if (user.isAuthenticated() && acl.can('transfer', user.role, accountId)) allowTransfer(); else deny();` Use appropriate cryptographic hashing for security-sensitive data WHAT: Misusing hashing and encryption interchangeably, or using weak/fast hashes (e.g., MD5) for passwords or other security-sensitive data, leads to easily guessable or reversible protections. WHY: Attackers can perform large-scale brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks if hashes are fast or weak, compromising passwords and integrity checks. HOW: Use modern, strong, and slow password-hashing/KDF algorithms (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) with high iteration counts; reserve fast hashes (e.g., SHA-256, BLAKE2) only for integrity checks where speed is needed and secrets are not protected by the hash alone. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure for passwords): `pwdHash := md5.Sum([]byte(password))` → After (safer): `pwdHash, err := argon2idKey([]byte(password), salt, timeCost, memoryCost, threads, keyLen)` Use authenticated encryption modes or high-level crypto abstractions WHAT: Using raw AES in non-authenticated modes (e.g., ECB/CBC without MAC) or hand-rolled constructions for encrypting sensitive data can allow undetected tampering and misuse of cryptography. WHY: Attackers may modify ciphertext without detection, leading to data corruption, privilege escalation, or bypass of security checks that rely on encrypted data. HOW: For symmetric encryption, use authenticated encryption modes such as AES-GCM or modern AEAD constructions (e.g., chacha20poly1305), or high-level libraries/abstractions like Go’s x/crypto/nacl/box or nacl/secretbox when they fit the use case; avoid implementing your own mode or combining ciphers and MACs manually. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): use AES-CBC/ECB directly for application data without integrity protection. After (safer): use crypto/aes with cipher.NewGCM (AES-GCM) or x/crypto/chacha20poly1305, or replace custom AES usage with nacl/secretbox for symmetric authenticated encryption. Nonce reuse and ciphertext layout in AEAD encryption WHAT: The same nonce slice is used as both the nonce and the destination buffer in `aead.Seal`, which can corrupt the stored nonce and ciphertext layout. WHY: Corrupted or reused nonces in AEAD (GCM) can break decryption and, in some cases, undermine confidentiality and integrity guarantees. HOW: Use a separate output buffer for `aead.Seal`, prepend the nonce explicitly to the ciphertext, and ensure each encryption call uses a fresh, random nonce of the correct size. EXAMPLE: Before (Go): `ciphertext := aead.Seal(nonce, nonce, val, nil)`; After (Go): `ciphertext := aead.Seal(nil, nonce, val, nil); out := append(nonce, ciphertext...)` Avoid hardcoded cryptographic keys in source code WHAT: Storing cryptographic keys or master secrets directly in source code (e.g., as string literals) exposes them to anyone with code or binary access. WHY: Compromised keys allow attackers to decrypt data, forge messages, or impersonate services, breaking confidentiality and integrity. HOW: Load keys from secure storage (KMS, environment variables, secrets manager), enforce a key-management policy, and restrict access to master secrets; rotate keys regularly and never commit them to version control. EXAMPLE (Go, before): `secret := []byte("hardcoded-secret-key")` EXAMPLE (Go, after): `secret := []byte(os.Getenv("APP_SECRET_KEY"))` Use cryptographically secure random generators for unguessable values WHAT: Using default or pseudo-random generators (e.g., math/rand with a fixed or predictable seed) for security-sensitive values (tokens, GUIDs, file names) makes outputs deterministic and guessable. WHY: Attackers can predict or reproduce these “random” values, enabling token forgery, session hijacking, or unauthorized access. HOW: For any value that must be unguessable, use a cryptographic RNG from the platform’s crypto module (e.g., crypto/rand in Go) instead of non-crypto PRNGs; never rely on default seeds or time-based seeding for security. EXAMPLE: Before (Go, insecure): `n := rand.Intn(1984)`; After (Go, secure): `n, _ := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(1984))`. Use cryptographically secure randomness for secrets WHAT: Using predictable pseudo-random generators (e.g., math/rand) for security-sensitive values (passwords, tokens, keys) allows attackers to predict those values. WHY: Predictable “random” values let attackers guess default passwords, session tokens, or keys, leading to account takeover and data compromise. HOW: For any secret or security token, use a cryptographically secure RNG (e.g., crypto/rand) that draws from OS randomness and cannot be seeded by application code. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `pwd := hash(strconv.Itoa(rand.Int()))` using math/rand; After (secure): use crypto/rand to generate random bytes and derive the password/token from those bytes. Error handling and logging WHAT: Missing or improper error handling and non-centralized logging can cause crashes, hide failures, and allow attackers to erase traces of their actions. WHY: Unhandled errors can lead to denial of service, and logs stored only locally can be deleted or tampered with, preventing detection and response to attacks. HOW: Always catch and handle errors that could crash the system, and send logs to a centralized, append-only logging service with restricted delete/modify permissions. EXAMPLE: Before: Application writes logs only to a local file on the same server. After: Application sends structured logs to a remote log aggregation service with role-based access controls and retention policies. Avoid leaking sensitive data in Go error handling and logging WHAT: Exposing detailed error messages, stack traces, or debug information (e.g., via fmt.Println, logs, or HTTP responses) that include sensitive data or internal details. WHY: Attackers can use leaked information (secrets, internal structure, stack traces) to escalate attacks, bypass controls, or compromise confidentiality. HOW: Sanitize and generalize error messages returned to users; log detailed errors only to secure logs; never include secrets, credentials, or internal implementation details in error messages; review error handlers to ensure they do not output stack traces or debug data in production. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `http.Error(w, err.Error(), 500)`; After (safer): `log.Printf("internal error: %v", err); http.Error(w, "internal server error", 500)` Safe use of panic, recover, defer, and log.Fatal in Go WHAT: Misusing panic/recover and log.Fatal (which calls os.Exit) can skip deferred cleanup (mutex unlocks, buffer flushes, temp file removal), leaving resources locked or data unflushed on errors. WHY: Skipped defers and cleanup can cause data loss, corrupted state, resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures in production. HOW: Use panic/recover for exceptional, recoverable failures and ensure critical cleanup is in defers that will run; use log.Fatal only for truly unrecoverable startup or non-interactive failures where immediate exit is desired and no further cleanup is required. EXAMPLE (Go): // Risky: log.Fatal skips deferred cleanup defer mu.Unlock() if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) // mu.Unlock never runs } // Safer: log error, return, or panic with recover handling so defers run defer mu.Unlock() if err != nil { log.Println(err) return } Fail-safe defaults for security errors WHAT: Failing to deny access by default when a security control errors, leading to unintended access being granted. WHY: If security checks fail open, attackers can bypass authentication/authorization or other controls when errors occur. HOW: Implement security checks so that any error, timeout, or unexpected condition results in access being denied; only explicitly validated and approved requests should be allowed. EXAMPLE: Before: `if err != nil { allowAccess() } else if ok { allowAccess() }`. After: `if err != nil || !ok { denyAccess() } else { allowAccess() }`. Secure logging and error handling WHAT: Application logging must be centrally controlled and must not expose sensitive data (e.g., passwords, session tokens, system details, stack traces) or detailed debug info, especially in error paths. WHY: Exposing sensitive data or internal details in logs or error messages can enable credential theft, session hijacking, privilege escalation, and targeted attacks. HOW: Implement a single, trusted logging routine in the application; classify and log both successful and failed security-relevant events; scrub or omit sensitive fields before logging; and present only generic error messages or custom error pages to users while recording detailed errors in restricted logs. EXAMPLE: Before (bad): `log.Printf("Login failed for user=%s, pwd=%s, stack=%v", user, pwd, err)`; After (good): `log.Printf("Login failed for user=%s, reason=%v", userID, errCode)` and show the user a generic message like `"Login failed. Please try again."` Secure logging and log integrity WHAT: Logs may be unusable for security monitoring, may be tampered with, or may cause unintended behavior if Fatal/Panic are misused or if log viewers execute untrusted log data as code. WHY: Missing or corrupted logs hinder incident response; tampered logs can hide attacks; executing untrusted log data can lead to code execution and system compromise. HOW: Use a logging library with levels/formatters suitable for SIEM; restrict log access to authorized users; ensure log viewers treat log content as data (no code execution of untrusted fields); use cryptographic hashes (e.g., SHA-256) stored in a protected location to verify log integrity before updates; understand and use Fatal/Panic semantics carefully to avoid losing buffered/temporary data. EXAMPLE: Before (integrity not checked): write logs directly without verification. After (integrity checked): compute SHA-256 of the log file, compare it against a securely stored checksum, and only then trust or update the log, storing the new checksum securely. Data protection and least privilege WHAT: Failure to enforce least-privilege roles and to securely handle temporary/cache files can expose sensitive data to unauthorized users or processes. WHY: Overly broad permissions or leftover sensitive files can lead to data disclosure, account compromise, or abuse of application/system functions. HOW: Define and enforce minimal roles and permissions for each user and system account; restrict access to only required functions and data; promptly delete temporary/cache files containing sensitive data or move them to protected storage and, if retained, encrypt them. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): all users share one admin role with full access and temp files with session data are left world-readable; After (secure): distinct roles (e.g., sales, marketing, developer) with scoped permissions, and temp/cache files containing sensitive data are either securely deleted after use or stored in an access-controlled, encrypted location. Sensitive data exposure in comments and URLs WHAT: Leaving sensitive endpoints or credentials in source-code comments, or passing secrets (API keys, tokens, session IDs, PINs) in HTTP GET query strings, exposes them via code, logs, browser history, proxies, and search engines. WHY: Attackers can recover these values from source control, comments, logs, intercepted traffic, or cached URLs and then impersonate users, call internal APIs, or escalate privileges. HOW: Never store real credentials or secret endpoints in comments; use configuration/secret management instead. Do not send sensitive data in URLs; send it in the request body or headers over HTTPS, and use short-lived, high-entropy tokens. Ensure logs and histories do not contain secrets. EXAMPLE (Go, before): req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "http://mycompany.com/api/mytoken?api_key=000s3cr3t000", nil) EXAMPLE (Go, after): req, _ := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://mycompany.com/api/mytoken", bytes.NewBuffer(body)); req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token) Protecting highly sensitive data with strong encryption WHAT: Storing passwords, connection strings, or other sensitive data in clear text or in non-cryptographically secure formats (including client-side embeds like Flash or compiled binaries) exposes secrets to attackers. WHY: Attackers who gain file, binary, or client access can read unencrypted secrets, leading to account compromise, data breaches, and full system takeover. HOW: Store all highly sensitive data only in encrypted form using well-vetted cryptographic libraries; derive keys securely (e.g., bcrypt/scrypt), manage keys separately from code, and never embed secrets directly in source, binaries, or client assets. EXAMPLE (Go): Instead of hardcoding `dbPassword := "P@ssw0rd"` in code, load an encrypted value from secure storage and decrypt it at runtime using `golang.org/x/crypto` primitives with a key stored in a protected configuration or secret manager. Disable unnecessary features and client-side storage for sensitive data WHAT: Failing to disable unneeded services, form autocomplete, or caching on sensitive pages can leak credentials or confidential data (e.g., via XSS or shared devices). WHY: Attackers can exfiltrate stored autocomplete values or cached responses, leading to credential theft, session hijacking, or disclosure of sensitive information. HOW: Turn off unused applications/services; for login or sensitive forms, set `autocomplete="off"` on the form or specific fields; for sensitive responses, send HTTP headers to prevent caching and storage. EXAMPLE: Before (HTML): `
`; After: ``. Before (HTTP): no cache headers; After (Go): `w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache, no-store"); w.Header().Set("Pragma", "no-cache")`. Secure communication channels WHAT: Unencrypted or insecure communication channels (e.g., HTTP, raw WebSockets, backend links) allow attackers to intercept and read traffic (MITM). WHY: Compromised channels expose sensitive data, credentials, and session information, enabling account takeover and data breaches. HOW: Use TLS (HTTPS/WSS) for all client-server and backend communications; enforce HSTS; disable weak ciphers/protocols; validate certificates; and prevent downgrade to insecure channels. EXAMPLE: Before: `http://api.example.com/data` → After: `https://api.example.com/data` with strict TLS configuration and certificate validation. Secure TLS/HTTPS configuration in Go WHAT: Risk of insecure HTTPS if TLS is misconfigured or multiple/nonstandard TLS implementations are used, or if HSTS is not enforced for HTTPS-only access. WHY: Misconfiguration can allow downgrade/MiTM attacks, loss of confidentiality, and integrity failures on supposedly “secure” channels. HOW: Use Go’s standard crypto/tls package and http.ListenAndServeTLS with properly managed certificates/keys; configure TLS securely in one central place; and add the Strict-Transport-Security header with an appropriate max-age and includeSubDomains for HTTPS endpoints. EXAMPLE: Before: (no HSTS) w.Write([]byte("...")) After: w.Header().Add("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains"); w.Write([]byte("...")) TLS configuration and certificate validation WHAT: Misconfigured TLS (invalid/expired certificates, wrong hostname, disabled verification, weak protocol versions) can lead to insecure connections and man-in-the-middle attacks. WHY: Attackers can impersonate servers, intercept or modify traffic, or downgrade connections to vulnerable ciphers/protocols (e.g., POODLE via SSLv3). HOW: Always use valid, non-expired certificates with correct domain names and required intermediates; never set InsecureSkipVerify to true in production; set the correct ServerName; explicitly configure MinVersion/MaxVersion to disallow obsolete protocols (e.g., SSLv3). EXAMPLE: config := &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: false, ServerName: "yourHostname", MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12} TLS/HTTP configuration and data handling WHAT: Misconfigured TLS/HTTP clients (weak protocol versions, insecure renegotiation, missing charset, leaking sensitive headers) can create insecure channels or expose confidential data. WHY: Attackers can exploit downgrade/renegotiation issues, compression side channels, or header leakage to read or manipulate sensitive information. HOW: Use only strong TLS versions/ciphers; verify cipher safety (e.g., via SSL Labs); rely on Go’s no-fallback behavior and absence of TLS compression unless adding external libraries; on renegotiation failures, use GetClientCertificate and abort on errors; always set a fixed charset (e.g., UTF-8) in Content-Type; strip sensitive data from HTTP headers for external requests. EXAMPLE: w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8") WebSocket Origin and Host Validation WHAT: Failure to validate the Origin and Host headers during the initial WebSocket HTTP handshake allows the server to accept connections from untrusted origins, enabling CSRF/CSWSH attacks. WHY: An attacker’s site can open a WebSocket to your server and perform actions as the victim, compromising confidentiality and integrity of user data and operations. HOW: On every WebSocket handshake, read the Origin header and compare it against an allowlist and/or the expected scheme+Host; reject the connection if the Origin is missing, malformed, or not explicitly trusted, and prefer wss:// (TLS) for sensitive data. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `websocket.Handler(EchoHandler).ServeHTTP(w, r)` After (safe): `if r.Header.Get("Origin") != "http://"+r.Host { http.Error(w,"Origin not allowed",403); return } else { websocket.Handler(EchoHandler).ServeHTTP(w,r) }` Secure use of WebSockets WHAT: Using unencrypted WebSockets (ws:// over port 80) or unsanitized data in WebSocket messages can leak session cookies and other sensitive data, and allow injection attacks. WHY: Attackers on the network can eavesdrop or tamper with traffic without TLS, and malicious payloads from untrusted sources can lead to XSS, injection, or data corruption. HOW: Always use wss:// (TLS) for WebSocket upgrades that carry cookies or other sensitive data, and apply strict input validation, sanitization, and output encoding to all data received from untrusted WebSocket clients before use. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `var ws = new WebSocket("ws://example.com/socket");` After (secure): `var ws = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/socket");` Directory listing exposure in Go web servers WHAT: Directory listings are unintentionally exposed when using http.FileServer(http.Dir(...)) and a directory has no index.html, allowing attackers to browse files. WHY: Attackers can discover and access sensitive files (backups, test data, configs) by navigating exposed directories. HOW: Disable directory listing by wrapping FileServer with a handler that rejects directory requests without an index file, and/or restrict served paths to only required static directories and files. EXAMPLE: Before: http.ListenAndServe(":8080", http.FileServer(http.Dir("/tmp/static"))) After: http.ListenAndServe(":8080", noDirListing(http.FileServer(http.Dir("/tmp/static")))) Minimize exposed functionality and information in production WHAT: Leaving unnecessary test code, files, or verbose HTTP response headers in production exposes internal implementation details and potentially sensitive information (e.g., OS, webserver, framework versions) to all users. WHY: Attackers can leverage exposed functionality and version details to identify known vulnerabilities, expand the attack surface, and gain easier paths to exploitation. HOW: Before deploying to production, remove or disable all test endpoints, debug routes, and non-essential files; ensure only required assets are publicly accessible; configure the web server/framework to omit or override headers that reveal OS, webserver, or language/framework versions. EXAMPLE: In production configuration, disable debug/test routes and strip identifying headers (e.g., in Nginx/Apache/app settings) so responses do not include `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, or similar version-disclosing headers. Web Application Information Disclosure and Hardening WHAT: Avoid disclosing framework/version details in HTTP headers and directory structure or admin paths in robots.txt, and ensure web server, processes, and service accounts run with least privilege and fail securely on errors. WHY: Version and path disclosure, excessive privileges, and verbose errors help attackers fingerprint your stack, find known exploits, and pivot through compromised components. HOW: Remove or avoid setting headers that reveal framework or version strings; restrict HTTP methods explicitly (e.g., via CORS) to only those needed; configure robots.txt with an allowlist of public paths and disallow everything else; configure least-privilege accounts for services; ensure error handling returns generic messages while logging details securely. EXAMPLE: Before (Go): w.Header().Set("X-Request-With", "Go Vulnerable Framework 1.2") After (Go): // Do not send framework/version header; only expose necessary headers. Asset Management Security Practices WHAT: Lack of systematic asset identification, classification, and risk assessment for software and system components can lead to unprotected or mismanaged assets and insecure configurations. WHY: Unmanaged or poorly classified assets may miss appropriate controls, increasing the risk of data breaches, service disruption, and non-compliance with security policies. HOW: Define an asset management scope, classify all software and system components by sensitivity and criticality, assess risks per asset, plan and implement risk mitigation, document applicable controls, train staff, and continuously monitor and improve the asset management system. Database server hardening for web applications WHAT: Unsecured database servers (default/root/anonymous accounts, test databases, unnecessary features) can be abused for unauthorized access, data theft, or privilege escalation. WHY: Attackers who reach a weakly configured DB server can bypass application controls, exfiltrate or modify data, and gain full system control. HOW: Set strong passwords for all root/administrative accounts; remove root accounts accessible from non-localhost; delete anonymous-user accounts, test databases, unnecessary stored procedures/services/content; install only required features; and disable all default accounts not used by the web app. EXAMPLE: Before: DB installed with default root password, anonymous users enabled, test DB present, all sample schemas and utilities installed. After: root password set and root restricted to localhost, anonymous users and test DB dropped, sample schemas/utilities removed, only required DB components installed, and a dedicated least-privilege app account created for connections. Safe use of Go database/sql with context WHAT: Failing to use context-aware database/sql methods (e.g., using Query instead of QueryContext with a proper Context) can leave queries and transactions running without timeouts or cancellation, and may delay returning connections to the pool. WHY: Unbounded or uncancellable database operations can exhaust the connection pool, leak resources, and degrade availability under load or when credentials/connectivity are wrong. HOW: Always use the context variants (e.g., QueryContext, ExecContext, BeginTx) with a Context that has appropriate deadlines/timeouts and cancellation; ensure operations return promptly so connections are released back to the pool. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `rows, err := db.Query("SELECT ...")` After (safer): `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second); defer cancel(); rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, "SELECT ...")` Connection string protection WHAT: Hard-coding database connection strings (including usernames/passwords) directly in source code exposes credentials if the code is shared or leaked. WHY: Exposed credentials can let attackers access databases, steal or modify data, or pivot further into the system. HOW: Store connection strings and authentication details in a separate, non-public configuration mechanism (e.g., environment variables or secured config files) and load them at runtime; never commit them to source control. EXAMPLE: Before: db, _ := sql.Open("mysql", "user:pass@/cxdb") After: dsn := os.Getenv("DB_DSN"); db, _ := sql.Open("mysql", dsn) Secure storage and use of database configuration and credentials WHAT: Storing database configuration and plaintext credentials in web-accessible or weakly protected locations, and reusing the same credentials across all trust levels, allows attackers who access the file or connection to gain full database privileges. WHY: Exposure or misuse of high-privilege credentials can lead to data theft, tampering, or full database compromise. HOW: Store configuration files outside web/public directories with strict filesystem permissions; encrypt configuration files at rest; never hardcode credentials in source; use distinct database accounts per trust level (e.g., read-only, user, admin) with least-privilege grants; ensure application connections use the minimum required role for each operation. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): configFile, _ := os.Open("/home/public_html/configDB.xml") and db, _ := sql.Open("mysql", "admin:AdminPass@/maindb"); After (more secure): configFile, _ := os.Open("/home/private/configDB.enc") with decryption in memory and db, _ := sql.Open("mysql", "readonly:ROpass@/maindb") for read-only operations, using a separate limited account for admin tasks. Database authentication and credential management WHAT: Using overly privileged database accounts, weak or default passwords, or exposing credentials (including private keys) in public repositories allows attackers to gain unauthorized read/write access to the database. WHY: Compromise of database credentials can lead to full data disclosure, data tampering, or complete takeover of the database server. HOW: Create least-privilege database users (e.g., read-only if writes are not needed), set strong unique passwords (use a password manager), change/remove default admin accounts and passwords, and never commit credentials or private keys to public version control. EXAMPLE: Before: using default `root` with no password in code and pushing it to GitHub. After: create a `report_reader` user with read-only rights, strong password stored in a secure secret manager, and ensure no credentials are present in the repository. Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when building SQL queries by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input instead of using parameterized queries or prepared statements. WHY: Attackers can inject arbitrary SQL, leading to data theft, corruption, or full compromise of the database. HOW: Always use prepared statements with bound parameters for any user-supplied values; only consider non-prepared queries if robust input validation and output encoding are implemented in a separate, enforced layer and the database truly cannot support prepared statements. EXAMPLE (Go, before): db.Exec("UPDATE creditcards SET name='" + customerName + "' WHERE customerId=233") EXAMPLE (Go, after): db.Exec("UPDATE creditcards SET name=? WHERE customerId=?", customerName, 233) Use stored procedures to restrict direct data access WHAT: Directly querying tables (e.g., `SELECT * FROM tblUsers WHERE userId = $user_input`) can expose sensitive columns (such as passport IDs) to application/database users who should not see them. WHY: Overly broad access lets users or compromised accounts read confidential data beyond what their role requires, increasing data‑leak and privacy‑breach risk. HOW: Define stored procedures that return only the necessary columns, grant applications/users EXECUTE permission on those procedures, and revoke/limit direct SELECT on underlying tables; combine this with proper input validation and least‑privilege DB roles. EXAMPLE: Before: `SELECT * FROM tblUsers WHERE userId = @userId;` After (procedure): `CREATE PROCEDURE db.getName @userId INT AS SELECT name, lastname FROM tblUsers WHERE userId = @userId; GRANT EXECUTE ON db.getName TO app_user; REVOKE SELECT ON tblUsers FROM app_user;` Secure file upload handling WHAT: User-controlled file uploads or file data are accepted without authentication, type validation, or safe storage, allowing arbitrary files to be stored in executable or web-accessible locations. WHY: Attackers can upload malicious content, trigger remote code execution, or serve malware to users if files are interpreted or executed by the server or clients. HOW: Allow uploads only from authenticated users; detect MIME type from file content (e.g., http.DetectContentType on a fixed-size buffer) and enforce an allowlist of accepted types; store uploaded files outside the web root on a non-executable volume or content server; on *NIX, use chroot or mount the upload directory as a separate logical drive without execute permissions. EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): accept any uploaded file and save it under the web root with default permissions. After (secure, Go): read first 512 bytes into buff, filetype := http.DetectContentType(buff), reject if filetype not in an allowlist (e.g., image/jpeg, image/png), and write the file to a non-executable directory outside the web context. Dynamic redirects and file handling WHAT: Dynamic redirects and file operations that use user-supplied data can lead to open redirects, path traversal, information disclosure, and remote code execution if absolute paths or unvalidated input are used. WHY: Attackers can redirect users to malicious sites, access or overwrite sensitive files, discover server filesystem structure, or execute arbitrary code via dynamically loaded plugins or uploaded files. HOW: Do not pass raw user data into redirect targets; if necessary, only accept validated data mapped to a predefined allowlist of relative paths or indices; never expose absolute file paths; set application files/resources to read-only; scan all uploaded files for malware; and never feed user-controlled data into dynamic loading/plugin mechanisms. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `http.Redirect(w, r, r.URL.Query().Get("next"), http.StatusFound)`; After (safe): `allowed := map[string]string{"home": "/home", "profile": "/user/profile"}; key := r.URL.Query().Get("next"); target, ok := allowed[key]; if !ok { target = "/home" }; http.Redirect(w, r, target, http.StatusFound)` Memory management and boundary checking WHAT: Risk of buffer overflows and out-of-bounds access when copying data or iterating over arrays/slices without checking destination size or collection length, leading to panics or memory corruption. WHY: Out-of-bounds writes/reads can cause crashes, data corruption, or exploitable memory-safety vulnerabilities; unclosed resources (files, connections) can cause leaks and denial of service. HOW: Always validate copy sizes against the destination buffer length; when looping, use the collection’s length as the upper bound; ensure all acquired resources (files, sockets, DB connections) are explicitly closed (e.g., via defer in Go) instead of relying solely on garbage collection. EXAMPLE: Before (Go): `for i := 0; i < 5; i++ { use(strings[i]) }` After: `for i := 0; i < len(strings); i++ { use(strings[i]) }` and `f, _ := os.Open(p); defer f.Close()` Avoid unsafe and manual memory management in Go WHAT: Using known-vulnerable functions or packages (e.g., unsafe, testing in production) or manually managing memory (custom allocators, disabling GC) can introduce memory corruption, data races, and undefined behavior. WHY: These practices can lead to exploitable vulnerabilities such as arbitrary code execution, data leakage, or denial of service in concurrent Go applications. HOW: Do not import or use the unsafe package or testing package in production code; rely on Go’s garbage collector for memory management; avoid disabling GC; only implement custom allocators (via syscall.Mmap or cgo malloc/free) when absolutely necessary and after rigorous review and testing. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe in production): `import "unsafe"` and using pointer arithmetic in live services; After: remove `unsafe` usage, refactor to safe Go constructs (slices, maps, channels) and rely on GC-managed memory. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Protection for State-Changing Requests WHAT: Failure to distinguish legitimate user-initiated state-changing requests from forged ones (e.g., changing recovery email via a simple GET/POST) allows attackers to trigger actions using the victim’s authenticated session. WHY: An attacker can trick users (e.g., via links in email/chat) into executing unintended actions, leading to account takeover or unauthorized state changes without stealing credentials. HOW: For every state-changing request, generate a per-session or per-request CSRF token when rendering the form/page, embed it as a form field, and verify it server-side before processing; reject requests with missing/invalid tokens and avoid using only cookies, URL parameters, or HTTPS as CSRF defenses. EXAMPLE: Before: `GET /account/recover?email=me@attacker.com` processed solely based on session cookie. After: Render form with hidden `csrf_token`, then on `POST /account/recover` validate `csrf_token` against the server-side value before updating the recovery email. CSRF Protection with Session-Bound Nonces/Tokens WHAT: Missing or improperly validated anti-CSRF tokens in state-changing requests (including GET, PUT, DELETE) allows attackers to trigger unauthorized actions on behalf of a user. WHY: An attacker can cause victims’ browsers to perform unintended operations (e.g., changing data, deleting resources) without their consent, leading to data loss or account compromise. HOW: For every state-changing request, require a cryptographically secure, large, random token that is unique per user session, validate its presence and correctness on the server, and use a well-tested framework’s built-in CSRF protection instead of custom code. EXAMPLE: Before: Accept POST/PUT/DELETE (or unsafe GET) requests without any CSRF token. After: Embed a framework-generated CSRF token in a hidden form field or header and verify it server-side for each state-changing request. CSRF protection for state-changing HTTP endpoints WHAT: Missing or incorrect CSRF protection on state-changing HTTP endpoints (e.g., POST /signup/post) allows attackers to trigger actions on behalf of authenticated users without their consent. WHY: An attacker can cause unauthorized state changes (account creation, data modification, transactions) by tricking a victim’s browser into sending forged requests with their cookies. HOW: Wrap routers/handlers for state-changing routes with a CSRF middleware, use a strong secret key, ensure tokens are generated per request/session, embed the CSRF token in forms or headers, and enable secure flags (e.g., csrf.Secure(true) in production). EXAMPLE (Go): Before: `http.ListenAndServe(":8000", r)` with form ``. After: `http.ListenAndServe(":8000", csrf.Protect([]byte("32-byte-long-auth-key"))(r))` and in template include `{{ .csrfField }}` so the POST to `/signup/post` includes a valid CSRF token. Regular expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) prevention WHAT: Avoid using regular expressions with catastrophic backtracking (e.g., nested quantifiers on overlapping patterns) for validating user-controlled input such as email addresses, as they can cause extremely slow matches and hang the application. WHY: Maliciously crafted input can trigger worst-case regex performance, leading to high CPU usage and Denial of Service (DoS) for the application. HOW: Prefer regex engines with guaranteed linear-time behavior (e.g., Go’s RE2); avoid complex patterns from untrusted sources; simplify patterns to remove nested quantifiers and ambiguous subexpressions; test regexes with large and adversarial inputs before deployment. EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable, catastrophic backtracking): `^([a-zA-Z0-9])(([\-.]|[_]+)?([a-zA-Z0-9]+))*(@){1}...$` (in a backtracking engine). After (safer): use a simpler email pattern and a linear-time engine like RE2, or delegate email validation to a well-reviewed library that guarantees no catastrophic backtracking. Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) in backtracking engines WHAT: Using complex or unbounded regular expressions in backtracking regex engines (e.g., JavaScript, PCRE) on attacker-controlled input can cause catastrophic backtracking and make the process hang. WHY: A hung process stops serving requests, leading to denial of service and potential business/availability loss. HOW: Avoid patterns with nested quantifiers or ambiguous groups on untrusted input; prefer regex engines like RE2 that avoid backtracking, or redesign patterns to be linear-time; enforce input length limits before matching. EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable, JS): `const regex = /^([a-zA-Z0-9])(([\-.]|[_]+)?([a-zA-Z0-9]+))*(@){1}[a-z0-9]+\.[a-z]{2,3}(\.[a-z]{2})?$/;` EXAMPLE: After (safer, JS): limit input length, simplify pattern to avoid nested `*`/`+`, or use a non-backtracking validator/library instead of a complex single regex. Regex backreferences for tag validation WHAT: Using regular expressions with backreferences to validate or parse nested or paired structures (e.g., HTML tags) can fail or behave unexpectedly across languages (e.g., Go does not support backreferences in its regexp engine), leading to incorrect validation logic. WHY: Incorrectly validated markup or structured input can allow malformed or malicious content to bypass checks, enabling injection, XSS, or content spoofing. HOW: Do not rely on regex backreferences to validate or parse structured or nested formats; instead, use a proper parser or a language/library that explicitly supports and correctly handles such constructs, and ensure tests cover malformed and mismatched cases. Regular expression engine safety when replacing RE2 WHAT: Using alternative regular expression engines (e.g., regexp2) instead of Go’s standard RE2-based regexp can remove RE2’s safety guarantees (such as linear-time execution), and may also change how escape sequences and backreferences are parsed, causing runtime panics or performance issues. WHY: Loss of RE2’s safety features can enable Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) and unexpected crashes, impacting availability and reliability. HOW: Prefer the standard RE2-based regexp package whenever possible; if a full-featured alternative is required, audit all patterns for catastrophic backtracking, validate and test escape sequences/backreferences, and add timeouts or input size limits around regex evaluation. Secure use of local preview and build tools WHAT: Running local preview/build commands (e.g., `npm run serve`, `docker-compose run ... build`) can expose services on `localhost` or execute untrusted project scripts that may be malicious or misconfigured. WHY: Malicious or misconfigured scripts can execute arbitrary code, exfiltrate data, or open unintended network ports, leading to local compromise or data leakage. HOW: Before running project-supplied commands, inspect `package.json`, Dockerfiles, and compose files; ensure scripts only perform expected actions, bind services to `127.0.0.1` with non-public ports, and run them under a non-privileged user in an isolated environment (e.g., dedicated user account or container). EXAMPLE: Before using `npm run serve`, review the `serve` script in `package.json` to confirm it only starts a local server on `127.0.0.1` and does not execute arbitrary shell commands or bind to external interfaces.
